Introduction

Ultrasound (in Chinese chāoshēng, which has nothing to do with the identically pronounced “excess births” of the classic comedy sketch “Excess-Birth Guerrillas”; I’m channeling the pun-loving stand-up comedian Wang Jianguo here and having a ball) is sound at frequencies above the upper limit of human hearing. Ultrasonics, a rising star in the acoustics family, was not clearly defined until the early 19th century. Today it is used widely in industry and medicine, in sonar, medical ultrasound, sonochemistry, nondestructive testing, materials characterization and more.

So what is ultrasound? How did it develop? What is it good for? And most importantly, what does it have to do with the Titanic? Patience, ladies and gentlemen: read on. I’ll cover the topic in detail under three headings: what ultrasound is, the history of ultrasonics and applications of ultrasound.

What is ultrasound?

Definition

As I said in the introduction, ultrasound is sound at frequencies above the highest threshold of human hearing (20 kHz). Human hearing generally spans 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and sound below 20 Hz is called infrasound. The frequency range of sound waves is generally taken to be 15 Hz to 1 THz (that T is the same T as on your hard drive: 10 to the power of 12). Above 1 GHz, sound is usually called hypersound, also known as “microwave acoustics” or “quantum acoustics,” because the sound behaves more like particles and its wave nature becomes less obvious. So wave–particle duality is not unique to light: it exists for sound as well.

The lower frequency limit of ultrasound is rather fuzzy and not necessarily 20 kHz. Some ultrasound research works with lower limits of 15–18 kHz, and you can hardly say that isn’t ultrasound. Conversely, some hi-fi enthusiasts insist on audio up to 25 kHz. So between audible sound and ultrasound there is an ambiguous zone of overlap.

Grab some decent headphones and test your hearing. I tried two phones: the iPhone has commanding bass and slightly weak treble; the Xiaomi’s bass is an utter failure, its treble slightly stronger. The audio in WeChat articles may also be compressed, which could affect the results.

Well, above 15 kHz I can’t hear a thing. Either my speakers are rubbish, or ↓↓

In terms of frequency, ultrasound is defined much like ultraviolet: electromagnetic waves at frequencies above visible light. No wonder Freddie Mercury of Queen couldn’t tell light from sound. Clearly his physics was taught by the music teacher.

Light and sound, one big family

“I’m travelling at the speed of light, I wanna make a supersonic man out of you”

Ultrasound in the real world

Humans can’t hear ultrasound, but the animal kingdom is full of ultrasound experts, including the bat, lately so notorious. Bats emit ultrasound and use the strength, delay and frequency shift of the echoes to work out roughly what objects are around them, how far away they are and how fast they are moving: the echolocation skill unlocked. Dolphins and submarines have the same skill pack installed. Sound is attenuated less in water than in air, so underwater animals can make even better use of echolocation.

Echolocation

[https://sensorlocalization.wordpress.com/tag/bat/]

Lots of animals can hear ultrasound. So if your cat or dog suddenly seems to see or hear something, don’t be scared. It is not the supernatural; they have most likely heard some ultrasound.

Dogs can hear sounds up to 35 kHz. Dog whistles exploit the fact that a dog’s upper hearing limit is higher than ours. Cats can hear even higher frequencies than dogs, and rats can hear ultrasound up to 100 kHz. Rats not only hear ultrasound; they also emit it when they are excited, for example when they are being tickled and loving it.

Ultrasound from a tickled rat, shifted down in frequency so that humans can hear it

To avoid being eaten, moths can hear ultrasound up to 200 kHz. They will go to any lengths for intelligence on the enemy (mainly bats; bats again).

If it’s all sound, just at higher frequencies, why single out ultrasound?

There are several reasons.

1. The main one is that at high frequencies, every structural element of a source has to be treated as a waveguide rather than simplified to masses and springs.

2. Accelerations, pressure variations, and intensities and energy densities are many orders of magnitude larger than for audible sound, so nonlinear phenomena appear. In some cavities, ultrasound can cause permanent changes in solid materials beyond their elastic range.

Here comedian Da Peng’s hands are going back and forth 30,000 times a second

3. Because its wavelength is short, ultrasound is extremely directional. This property is widely exploited in nondestructive testing of materials and in medical diagnosis.

4. Ultrasound has great advantages for probing the physical properties of matter and the atomic and molecular structure of solids and liquids.

A history of ultrasonics

The history of ultrasonics can be divided at World War I (1914–1918). Before then, there were only a handful of ways to generate ultrasound, and little research on it.

t < World War I

Before World War I there were two big pieces of news in ultrasonics, and both drove its later development:

the discovery of magnetostriction and of the piezoelectric effect. The first was discovered by Joule in 1847 (yes, that Joule, the J that is full of energy), the second by the Curie brothers (not Madame Curie) in 1880.

Now back to the question from the introduction: what does ultrasound have to do with the Titanic? Was the title just clickbait?

t > World War I

Why mention the Titanic? Because one week after the Titanic sank, Lewis Richardson filed a patent for ultrasonic echolocation and ranging, which marks the beginning of modern ultrasonics research. Then World War I broke out, and the need to detect submarines drove the development of underwater acoustics. Sonar (sound navigation and ranging) was developed during this period. The British scientist Robert William Boyle was the main force behind it. Interestingly, he published the first review article on ultrasonics in 1928; unfortunately, the journal folded right after it came out, so the review had limited impact. Attention, researchers! If you sweat blood over a review, submit it to a reliable journal. Paul Langevin successfully commercialized underwater ultrasound and had ultrasonic ranging equipment fitted to many ships.

Research can make more than your hair disappear: your published papers can vanish too

After World War I ended, ultrasonics gradually faded, until the invention of the ultrasonic interferometer in 1925, a major breakthrough for ultrasonics in physical acoustics. In 1927 the American scientists Robert Williams Wood and Alfred Lee Loomis together developed high-intensity ultrasound and studied many effects of ultrasound at high intensities. Wood had it even worse than Langevin mentioned above: he finished his doctoral thesis, then the University of Chicago changed its academic rules, and he never got his PhD in his whole life. So besides your hair and your papers, your PhD can vanish too. Wood and Loomis also studied the biological effects of ultrasound, publishing on everything from bacteria to fruit flies. Besides acoustics, Loomis worked mainly in optics, and he was a pioneer of EEG (electroencephalography) and GPS.

During World War II, applications of ultrasound became more mature and widespread and gradually spread into medicine. With the development of electronics, ultrasonics reached its first peak. High-intensity ultrasound was used for cleaning, already at an industrial scale. In the early 1940s, the invention of the pulse-echo method brought ultrasound into nondestructive testing of materials. In the 1950s the first B-mode ultrasound scanners appeared, the beginning of modern ultrasound diagnostics.

From the 1970s on, ultrasonics covered an ever wider range of fields. The rapid development of computing and electronics gave it an enormous boost. Yet however it develops, its core has always been physics. Like acoustics as a whole, ultrasonics has become increasingly multidisciplinary. By 2005 more than 10,000 papers related to ultrasound had been published, across all sorts of fields. You can find ultrasound in imaging, process monitoring, biochemistry, medical diagnosis and therapy, bioengineering, nanotechnology, veterinary medicine and defense.

Applications of ultrasound

After the “wheel of acoustics” (What is acoustics, anyway?), meet the “wheel of ultrasonics.”

The wheel of ultrasonics

This summary comes from an article from the 1970s, and it covers most areas of ultrasonics. There are five main categories:

Materials science: nondestructive testing, welding, atomization, emulsification and so on;

Engineering: sonar, electronic communications, metal forming, structural monitoring and so on;

Metrology: imaging, acoustic microscopy, and measurement of quantities such as flow velocity, density and viscosity;

Chemistry: sample preparation, sonochemical reactions, process monitoring and so on;

Biology: medicine, bubble detection and so on.

The medical side was covered in detail in an earlier article in this column:

What’s that sticky gel they put on your belly for an ultrasound? An introduction to biomedical ultrasound

Medical diagnosis

[https://www.verywellhealth.com/ultrasound-application-techniques-2696542]

From another angle, that of industry, the applications can be grouped as in the figure below into three classes: processing, nondestructive testing, and measurement and control.

Here are a few animations showing some classic industrial applications of ultrasound.

Ultrasonic cleaning: the high frequency of ultrasound agitates a liquid rapidly and cleans whatever is in it. Easy to picture: if you could scrub your laundry more than 20,000 times a second… the clothes would be scrubbed out of existence, so of course they’d be clean…

Ultrasonic cleaning: keep an eye out for it next time you visit an optician

[https://www.medgadget.com/2018/05/smartclean-vision-5-a-portable-ultrasonic-cleaner.html]

Nondestructive testing: using the high directivity of ultrasound, anomalies in the reflected pulse waveforms reveal whether the material under test is damaged.

Nondestructive testing

[https://www.tec-science.com/material-science/material-testing/ultrasonic-testing-ut/]

Beyond the traditional applications, I have recently come across some ultrasonic wizardry that I’d like to single out.

Graphene ultrasonic transducers

In 2015, American scientists built an ultrasonic transmitter and receiver out of graphene that can be used for wireless communication. The device can reportedly transmit high-fidelity audio over a broad band from 20 Hz to 0.5 MHz, and it can record the ultrasound emitted by bats.

http://www.cas.cn/kj/201507/t20150709_4387182.shtml

Virtual buttons

A tiny ultrasonic sensor can turn anything into a button. The sensor detects gestures and does the job of a button. If this really reaches industrial use, the change will be earth-shattering. Imagine how crazy a world without buttons would be!

The arrow points to the ultrasonic sensor, next to an ordinary coin

[https://www.ultrasensesys.com/applications#Applications-hero]

Virtual headphones

This is something a former colleague is working on, and I think it’s very cool: a hybrid of headphones, loudspeakers and 3D audio reproduction that keeps the best of each and discards the rest. It rests on three principles:

1. A 3D sensor identifies the position of the head, and of the ears in particular;

2. Highly directional sound is beamed at the ears. Once the positions of the ears are known, the binaural audio signals are modulated onto ultrasound, allowing precision strikes on each ear. Some nonlinear, self-demodulating algorithm (I don’t know what it is; if you do, please enlighten me) then recovers the original audio at the ears;

3. The ultrasound is emitted by a special loudspeaker, a multi-cell speaker module.

Audio modulated onto ultrasound and demodulated, then received by the ear [https://www.focusonics.com/technology/]

You wear nothing, yet you get the effect of headphones. And it does something loudspeakers can’t match: virtual headphones can make a sound audible to the intended listener only, and to no one else. The implications for public spaces are huge. Different areas of a museum room could play different audio for different exhibits without interfering with each other; a family of three in a car could each listen to their own music without headphones; and in an open-plan office you could take calls and video meetings without headphones and without disturbing anyone.

Private sound zones

The concept is very attractive, though I don’t know how well it works in practice. I’m curious how they deal with several issues: the accuracy of ear tracking; whether ultrasound can deliver the sound right to the entrance of the ear canal; how errors in delivery position and tracking make the HRTFs inaccurate and degrade the binaural experience; and how to keep the demodulated sound from spreading into the surroundings.

References

[1] Kuttruff, H. (Ed.). (2012). Ultrasonics: Fundamentals and applications. Springer Science & Business Media.

[2] Ensminger, D., & Bond, L. J. (2011). Ultrasonics: fundamentals, technologies, and applications. CRC Press.

[3] https://acousticstoday.org/the-dawn-of-ultrasonics-and-the-palace-of-science-kenneth-s-suslick/

[4] Zhou, Q., Zheng, J., Onishi, S., Crommie, M. F., & Zettl, A. K. (2015). Graphene electrostatic microphone and ultrasonic radio. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112(29), 8942–8946.
